newsitem.title: UK: New class of drug offers new hope against AIDS.
newsitem.headline: New class of drug offers new hope against AIDS.

text.p: AIDS doctors already given hope of combating the disease by new types of drugs and hard-hitting "cocktails" said on Wednesday they were getting even more encouragement from yet a new class of drug.

The drugs, known as non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs), had shown remarkable effects, researchers told the Third International Congress on Drug Therapy in HIV Infection, being held in Birmingham.
The drugs not only add a new weapon to the growing armoury against the HIV virus, but work as well as the highly touted protease inhibitors, Dr Julio Montaner of the Canadian HIV Trials Network said.
"I think it is a very major development," Montaner told Reuters in an interview.
Mark Wainberg and colleagues at Montreal's McGill University AIDS centre studied the effects of AZT and Bristol Myers Squibb's ddI combined with Boehringer Ingelheim's NNRTI nevirapine (Viramune).

"The use of triple drug therapy has led to non-detectable levels of virus in plasma (blood) in over 75 percent of patients who were previously drug-naive (had not been given any drugs)," Wainberg told the conference.
The effects remained 18 months later, he said. All 151 patients in the trial were still alive.
Joep Lange and colleagues at Amsterdam's Academic Medical Centre, working with Boehringer, found similar results.
"The triple therapy was clearly superior by 12 months," they reported. "Nevirapine provides new opportunities for combination treatment."

Montaner said the NNRTIs offered new choices to AIDS patients taking one or two drugs who suffered a resurgence of the virus. Once the virus mutates into a resistant form, doctors fear it will resist other drugs in the same class.
But having a new class of drugs to give the patients mean they have not used up all their opportunities for treatment.
Montaner said NNRTIs cost about half what most protease inhibitors did, but offered similar effects. Nevirapine was taken in two doses a day of two pills each, making it easy for patients to take.
All AIDS experts agree that what they call compliance -- taking the drugs every day at the right time -- is of paramount importance. The drugs all start to wear off after just a few hours.

The next stage will be to try a combination of four different drugs -- two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors such as Glaxo's AZT and 3TC or Bristol-Myer Squibb's D4T, a protease inhibitor such as Abbott Laboratories' ritonavir or Roche's saquinavir and an NNRTI.

But the NNRTIs and the protease inhibitors interfere with one another and drug companies must work to overcome this, said Dr David Ho of the Aaron Diamond AIDS Research Centre at New York's Rockefeller University.
"You have to get the companies to work together," he said.
AIDS researchers offered new hope to patients this summer when they announced that hitting the virus hard with a combination of drugs could knock it back to undetectable levels in the blood.
Each class of drug attacks the virus at a slightly different point in its cycle of replication.
